records.sourceFile: Relating American football age of first exposure to patient-reported outcomes and medical diagnoses among former National Football League player.pdf

paper.citation: Lempke LB, Walton SR, Brett BL, et al. Relating American Football Age of First Exposure to Patient-Reported Outcomes and Medical Diagnoses Among Former National Football League Players: An NFL-LONG study. Sports Med. 2022.
paper.abstract: In a cross-sectional survey of 1,784 former NFL players, earlier age of first exposure to football was associated with higher PROMIS scores for anxiety, depression, sleep disturbance, pain interference and emotional-behavioral dyscontrol, but with small effect sizes. AFE was not associated with self-reported anxiety, depression, dementia or mild cognitive impairment, and no AFE-by-age interaction was found.
paper.tldr: Among former NFL players, starting football earlier was linked only weakly to worse self-reported mood, sleep and pain scores and to none of the listed diagnoses. Age had much stronger associations with every outcome than AFE did.
paper.methods: Cross-sectional survey of former NFL players recruited through the NFL Alumni Association and team contacts (2019 to 2020). The questionnaire recorded AFE, football history and self-reported diagnoses. PROMIS and Neuro-QOL measures were analysed with multivariable linear regression, and diagnoses with Poisson regression for prevalence ratios, both including AFE, age and an AFE-by-age term that was dropped when not significant. Concussion history and total years of football were not adjusted for, as the authors judged them endogenous.
paper.findings: Among 1,784 players, one-year-later AFE was associated with lower PROMIS anxiety (B=-0.22, p=0.016), depression (B=-0.22, p=0.010), sleep disturbance (B=-0.16, p=0.007), pain interference (B=-0.19, p=0.014) and Neuro-QOL emotional-behavioral dyscontrol (B=-0.22, p=0.019). AFE showed no main effect on PROMIS cognitive function (p=0.116) or physical function (p=0.860) in Table 2, or on any diagnosis (anxiety, depression, dementia, mild cognitive impairment; all p>=0.449). Age was associated with all outcomes and diagnoses, and no AFE-by-age interaction was found (p>=0.066 for PROMIS, p>=0.147 for diagnoses).
paper.limitations: Outcomes and diagnoses were self-reported, participation was voluntary, and the sample was recruited through networks, so selection and survivorship bias are likely. Concussion history and total years of football were not adjusted for. Effects were small (R2 0.03 to 0.06). The results text gives p>=0.168 for cognitive and physical function while Table 2 gives p=0.116 and 0.860, and the conclusions list both as associated with AFE; the table values (not significant) were used here. The abstract says binomial regression while the methods describe Poisson regression.
paper.practicalImplications: Clinicians counselling former players can say that age of first exposure had at most a small association with self-reported mood, sleep and pain, and no measurable association with the listed diagnoses in this sample. The authors point to prior work in this cohort on modifiable factors such as exercise, diet and sleep, but those factors were not tested in this analysis.
paper.athleteDev: Performance Application: the study does not address performance. It shows that age of first exposure is a weak correlate of later self-reported function in retired professionals, so it cannot establish a safe or unsafe starting age for tackle football.
paper.rtp: Return to Sport Application: not applicable. The study covers retired players and does not examine injury, rehabilitation or return to sport, so it cannot inform return-to-play decisions.

records.sourceFile: Repetitive head injuries in German American football players do not change blood-based biomarker candidates for CTE during a single season.pdf

paper.citation: Bastgen, T., Evers, J., Oedekoven, C., Weide, C., Herzog, L., Ashton, N., et al. Repetitive head injuries in German American football players do not change blood-based biomarker candidates for CTE during a single season. Neurological Research and Practice. 2024;6:13.
paper.abstract: The authors measured seven blood-based candidate biomarkers for chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE) in 18 American football players before and after one season, and in 18 matched controls. Biomarker levels did not change significantly over the season. Phosphorylated tau was generally higher in players, and several biomarkers correlated with depression, quality of life, career length, training participation and headache after concussion.
paper.tldr: Across one football season, blood levels of the candidate CTE markers did not change significantly. Phosphorylated tau was higher in players than controls, but the study is too small to show what this means.
paper.methods: Eighteen male American football players gave blood before (T0) and after (T1) a season, and 18 sex- and age-matched controls gave blood once. Seven markers were measured (total tau, phosphorylated tau, neurofilament light, GFAP, amyloid-beta 40 and 42, and S100-B) with Simoa or ELISA-based assays. Apathy (AES-C), depression (BDI-II), EQ-5D-5L quality of life and a questionnaire on career, training and concussion history were collected. Group and time comparisons used Wilcoxon, Mann-Whitney and t-tests, and clinical correlations used Pearson correlation.
paper.findings: Phosphorylated tau was higher in players than controls at T0 (10.87 vs 6.39 pg/ml) and T1 (10.12 pg/ml), with no change across the season. Total tau rose slightly across the season but was not significant. Amyloid-beta 40 and 42 were lower in players, not significantly. GFAP, S100-B and neurofilament light did not differ significantly between groups or across the season. Correlations included lower amyloid-beta 42 with depression (T0 and T1) and with high training participation (T1), higher neurofilament light with depression (T1), higher total tau at T1 in players with 6 or more seasons, a positive correlation between GFAP and quality of life, and higher S100-B when players continued to play with headache after concussion in at least half of cases. Some correlations were based on very small subgroups (for example n = 3 for depression).
paper.limitations: The sample was small and the correlations used subgroups of as few as three players. The Methods report that three players dropped out after T0 with listwise deletion, yet the Results report n = 18 at T1, so the handling of dropouts is unclear. The training-participation threshold is 85% in the Results and 80% in the Discussion and Table 1. The text reports a positive GFAP and quality-of-life correlation, while Table 1 marks GFAP as decreased with higher quality of life. The authors describe the findings as indicative only, and blood markers may differ from cerebrospinal fluid markers, where earlier changes were reported.
paper.practicalImplications: Candidate CTE blood markers did not change over one season in this small group of players, so the study gives no basis for using a single-season blood check to track CTE risk. Phosphorylated tau was higher in players than controls, but the study does not show that this has any clinical meaning. These markers should not be used for diagnosis or return decisions, and repeated long-term monitoring is the authors' suggested next step.
paper.athleteDev: This paper does not inform performance training. It measured no performance, training-load or physical outcomes, and its only training link is an exploratory correlation between training attendance and amyloid-beta 42, which is too small to act on.
paper.rtp: This study cannot inform return to sport. It did not assess return-to-play decisions or recovery after concussion, and its headache-after-concussion correlation is exploratory and based on a small sample.

records.sourceFile: Repetitive head-injury exposure and later-in-life cognitive and emotional outcomes among former collegiate football players - A CLEAATS investigation.pdf

paper.citation: Schaffert, J., Datoc, A., Sanders, G. D., Didehbani, N., LoBue, C., & Cullum, C. M. Repetitive head-injury exposure and later-in-life cognitive and emotional outcomes among former collegiate football players: a CLEAATS investigation. International Review of Psychiatry. 2024;36(3):233-242.
paper.abstract: The authors examined how head-injury exposure measures relate to later-life subjective and objective cognition and emotional symptoms in 216 former collegiate football players aged 50 to 87. The cumulative exposure index did not predict any outcome. Diagnosed concussions had small associations with depression and subjective cognitive symptoms, and emotional symptoms were strongly associated with subjective cognitive complaints.
paper.tldr: In older former college players, cumulative head-injury exposure did not predict cognition or mood. Current mood symptoms were strongly linked to self-reported memory and thinking complaints, so mood should be considered when a former player reports cognitive problems.
paper.methods: Former male collegiate football players (n = 216, aged 50 to 87) from the CLEAATS study completed a survey on playing history, diagnosed concussions and symptomatic hits, and a head-injury exposure index was calculated from high school and college contact practice, games and position. Subjective cognition was measured with the Cognitive Functioning Instrument (CFI), objective cognition with the modified Telephone Interview for Cognitive Status (TICS-m, n = 157), and mood with the PHQ-8, GAD-7 and NQoL Emotional and Behavioral Dyscontrol scale. Hierarchical linear regressions were adjusted for age and education, and a p < .01 threshold was used.
paper.findings: The head-injury exposure index did not predict TICS-m, CFI, PHQ-8, GAD-7 or NQoL EBD (all p > .169). Each diagnosed concussion was associated with a small increase in PHQ-8 depressive symptoms (b = 0.50, p = .002, R2 change 0.052) and CFI subjective cognitive symptoms (b = 0.38, p = .002, R2 change 0.051). The emotional index was strongly associated with CFI scores (b = 0.69, p < .001, R2 = 0.36) but not with TICS-m scores (p = .052). When emotional symptoms were controlled, the concussion and CFI association was no longer significant (p = .078). Symptomatic hits were associated only with the NQoL EBD measure of emotional dysregulation (p = .006, R2 change 0.042).
paper.limitations: The design is cross-sectional and survey-based, so reverse causation is possible, as the authors note, since depression may increase reports of past concussions and symptoms. Concussion history and playing exposure are self-reported and recalled. The sample is male, well-educated and mostly White, and the cognitive measure was a brief telephone screen rather than full neuropsychological testing. Some analyses had missing data, and the authors describe the effects as small. The abstract and Results disagree on mean age (63.4 vs 64.1) and percentage White (91% vs 92%).
paper.practicalImplications: Self-reported subjective cognitive complaints in former players were strongly linked to current mood symptoms and were not significantly related to objective screening scores. Clinicians assessing a former player's cognitive complaints should consider current mood symptoms and objective testing, and should not rely on self-report alone. Head-injury exposure measures did not predict later cognition or mood in this group.
paper.athleteDev: This study does not inform performance training. Its participants were former collegiate players aged 50 and older, and none of its measures concerned current training, load or performance.
paper.rtp: This study cannot inform return to sport. It did not assess current injury, rehabilitation or return-to-play decisions, and its concussion results concern long-term symptoms and mood in retired players, which should not be applied to a current athlete's return decision.

records.sourceFile: Retired National Football League players are not at greater risk for suicide.pdf

paper.citation: Iverson GL. Retired National Football League Players are Not at Greater Risk for Suicide. Arch Clin Neuropsychol. 2020;35:332-341.
paper.abstract: Narrative review of the literature from 1928 to 2018 on suicide in former NFL players and its association with CTE. Epidemiological studies show lower suicide rates than in the general population, while a minority with depression and chronic pain appears to be at higher risk.
paper.tldr: Former NFL players as a group have lower suicide rates than men in the general population, so CTE should not be assumed to drive suicide risk. A subgroup with depression, chronic pain or financial stress is at real risk and should receive standard depression and suicide care.
paper.methods: Narrative review of the literature published from 1928 to 2018. No systematic search strategy is described. The review covers historical CTE case series, proposed clinical criteria, epidemiological cohorts of former NFL players and surveys of their mental health.
paper.findings: Suicide was not a recognized clinical feature of CTE in the literature before 2010. In a cohort of former NFL players followed to 2013, suicide was less common than expected against the US population (standardized mortality ratio 0.47; 12 of 537 deaths from intentional self-harm). Surveys show that a substantial minority of former players have depression, chronic pain and opioid use, which the author links to higher risk of suicidal thoughts.
paper.limitations: Narrative review with no described search or appraisal method, so study selection could be biased. The conclusions rest on cited case series, surveys and cohorts, and the review does not test whether CTE pathology changes suicide risk.
paper.practicalImplications: Treat former players with chronic pain, depression, substance abuse problems, life stress or financial difficulty as at increased risk of suicidal thoughts and behaviors, and offer evidence-based treatment. Avoid assuming that depression or suicidality is caused by CTE, because the author warns a CTE diagnosis could adversely affect treatment.
paper.athleteDev: No performance application. The review covers the mental health of retired players and does not test training, performance or readiness.
paper.rtp: Not applicable to return to sport. The review concerns retired players rather than active injury management, so it cannot inform return-to-play decisions after concussion or other injury.

records.sourceFile: Return to play and risk of repeat concussion in collegiate football players- comparative analysis from the NCAA Concussion Study (1999–2001) and CARE Consortium (2014–2017).pdf

paper.citation: McCrea M, Broglio S, McAllister T, Zhou W, Zhao S, Katz B, et al. Return to play and risk of repeat concussion in collegiate football players: comparative analysis from the NCAA Concussion Study (1999-2001) and CARE Consortium (2014-2017). Br J Sports Med. 2019.
paper.abstract: This comparative analysis of two cohorts of concussed NCAA football players (1999-2001 and 2014-2017) examined symptom recovery, the symptom-free waiting period, return to play and repeat concussion. Current players had longer symptoms, waiting periods and return times, and very few had a repeat concussion within 10 days of the first.
paper.tldr: Collegiate football players in the CARE Consortium were held out of play for longer than players in the earlier NCAA study, and far fewer had a repeat concussion within 10 days. The overall repeat-concussion rate difference was not statistically significant.
paper.methods: Concussed NCAA football players from the NCAA Concussion Study (n=184) and CARE Consortium (n=701) were compared for symptom duration, symptom-free waiting period (SFWP), return-to-play time and same-season repeat concussion. Missing values were handled by multiple imputation for CARE, and groups were compared with t tests, Wilcoxon tests and chi-square or Fisher exact tests.
paper.findings: Median symptom duration was 5.92 days in CARE and 2.00 days in the NCAA Study, median SFWP was 6.00 and 0.98 days, and mean return to play was 16.08 and 6.67 days (all P<0.0001). Same-season repeat concussion was 3.85% (27 of 701) in CARE and 6.52% (12 of 184) in the NCAA Study (P=0.17), while repeat concussion within 10 days was 1 of 27 in CARE and 11 of 12 in the NCAA Study (P<0.0001).
paper.limitations: The cohorts are non-randomised and about 15 years apart, so the effect of specific clinical practices cannot be isolated from changes in awareness, reporting, diagnosis, rules or equipment. Acute injuries looked more severe in the NCAA Study (LOC or PTA 28.3% vs 17.9%), recovery relied on athlete self-report, and the samples cover NCAA football players only. The overall repeat-concussion difference was not significant (P=0.17), so the 41% lower rate should not be read as a firm reduction.
paper.practicalImplications: The findings are consistent with international consensus advice to use a symptom-free waiting period and graded return, since repeat concussions within the first 10 days were rare in the CARE cohort, though the design cannot prove that the longer hold-out caused this. The overall same-season repeat rate did not differ significantly between eras.
paper.athleteDev: Performance staff can expect current collegiate players to be out for about two weeks on average after concussion, which should be built into training and competition planning. The findings are about clinical management, and the study does not evaluate training load or performance after return.
paper.rtp: The median return-to-play time of 12.23 days in CARE (IQR 8.04 to 18.92) and the finding that over 97% of CARE athletes had a symptom-free waiting period of at least one day can inform return timelines. The study shows group patterns in an observational setting and cannot set an individual's return date, so it should be used alongside the athlete's symptom and clinical assessment.
